what_its_for: Rosuvastatin is used to lower bad cholesterol (LDL) and fats (triglycerides) in your blood, while raising good cholesterol (HDL). It helps reduce your risk of heart attack, stroke, and other heart problems. It belongs to a group of medicines called statins.
how_to_take: Take rosuvastatin by mouth once a day, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole. If you are taking the capsule form (Ezallor Sprinkle), you can open it and sprinkle the contents onto a teaspoon of applesauce and swallow right away — do not chew or save it for later. Take it at the same time every day to help you remember. You can take it in the morning or at night — whichever works best for you.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your cholesterol levels and other health factors. The usual starting dose for adults is 10 mg to 20 mg once daily. Doses range from 5 mg to 40 mg per day. Do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first. The 40 mg dose is only used for people who have not reached their cholesterol goal on a lower dose.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — as long as it is the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regular time. Do not take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store rosuvastatin at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking large amounts of grapefruit juice while taking rosuvastatin, as it may increase the amount of medicine in your blood. Avoid drinking excessive amounts of alcohol, as it can raise your risk of liver problems. Avoid taking antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium within 2 hours of taking rosuvastatin, as they can lower how well the medicine works. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, especially blood thinners (like warfarin), cyclosporine, or niacin.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you experience: unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, weakness, or cramps (especially with fever or unusual tiredness) — this could be a sign of a rare but serious muscle problem called rhabdomyolysis; dark or cola-colored urine; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); severe stomach pain; or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. Also contact your doctor if you notice memory problems, confusion, or increased blood sugar levels.
when_it_works: Rosuvastatin begins lowering your cholesterol within 1 to 2 weeks of starting treatment. However, it may take 4 weeks or longer to see the full effect. Your doctor will likely check your cholesterol levels with a blood test about 4 to 12 weeks after you start. Remember, you may not feel any different, but the medicine is still working. Keep taking it every day as prescribed, even if you feel fine. This medicine works best when combined with a heart-healthy diet and regular exercise.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do not take rosuvastatin if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It may harm your unborn baby or nursing infant. Use effective birth control while taking this medicine and talk to your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Older adults (65 and older): Use with caution, as older adults may have a higher risk of muscle problems. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease. Rosuvastatin is not recommended for people with active liver disease. Lower doses may be needed for those with severe kidney problems. Asian patients: Asian patients may have higher blood levels of rosuvastatin, so your doctor may start you on a lower dose (5 mg).
